newsitem.title: PERU: Anti-Fujimori protestors clash with Peru police.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Fujimori protestors clash with Peru police.

text.p: Thousands of Peruvian workers marched on President Alberto Fujimori's residence on Thursday, chanting slogans against the embattled president and fighting with police who tried to block their way, witnesses said.

The workers, tossing stones and chanting "Down With The Dictatorship," clashed with about 300 police as they burst into the main square opposite Fujimori's Government Palace, which serves both as his residence and office.
There were no injuries immediately reported.

Four lines of about 500 heavily-armed riot policemen cordoned off Government Palace, where Fujimori was present, while soldiers stood on the roof watching the estimated 3,000 demonstrators, whose numbers were swelling quickly.
A police helicopter flew overhead, as workers swarmed into the Plaza de Armas square opposite the palace and over a large fountain in the centre.

"It's a good thing there are Peruvians who have the dignity to reject all this ill-treatment from the Fujimori government," said Juan Jose Gorriti, secretary-general of the Peruvian General Workers' Confederation that organised the march.
He was demanding an audience with Fujimori.
The march followed the resignation of at least two ministers from Fujimori's cabinet, deepening a political crisis that has seen the president's popularity plunge to the lowest level in seven years.
The workers, joined by students, chanted "Fujimori, out of the country!", "Out with the corrupt ones!" and "The dictatorship is going to fall!"

During seven years of power, Fujimori has maintained a traditionally high level of popularity due to his virtual defeat of leftist guerrillas and his economic reforms. But his approval rating has plunged in recent months to a new low of 23 percent.

Analysts say a series of allegations of human rights violations and corruption allegations against Fujimori's government and security forces, combined with continued deep poverty and high unemployment levels, are the main factors behind the public ire.
"We are dying of hunger. This dictatorship has to fall," protesting oil worker Maura Silva told Reuters.
"The government has to realise that its policies are tiring the workers," added opposition congressman Javier Diez Canseco.

Two pensioners joined the protest dressed up as armed forces head Gen. Nicolas Bari de Hermoza and security adviser Vladimiro Montesinos. Both men have been cited in recent polls as the men most Peruvians believe wield the real power of state.
